quotes.quote: Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on 2025 USA Math Olympiad
Ivo Petrov , Jasper Dekoninck , Lyuben Baltadzhiev , Maria Drencheva , Kristian Minchev , Mislav Balunović , Nikola Jovanović , Martin Vechev
[Submitted on 27 Mar 2025 ( v1 ), last revised 4 Sep 2025 (this version, v5)]
Using expert human annotators, we evaluated several state-of-the-art reasoning models on the six problems from the 2025 USAMO within hours of their release.
only Gemini-2.5-Pro achieves a non-trivial score of 25%, while all other models achieve less than 5%
We selected the USAMO 2025, a highly prestigious mathematics competition comprising six proofbased problems administered over two days, as our benchmark.
This competition aligns perfectly with our evaluation objectives, as the questions are challenging, require detailed proofs for full credit, and are uncontaminated.
we provided each model with the problems, prompting them explicitly to produce comprehensive and detailed proofs formatted in LATEX
To reduce variance, each model solved every problem four separate times.
Solutions, excluding thought traces, were anonymized and converted into PDF format for grading.

Our grading team consisted of four experts, each having substantial mathematical problem-solving experience as former national IMO team members or having participated in final-stage team selection processes for their countries.
Each of the six problems from USAMO 2025 was independently evaluated by two evaluators, with each judge responsible for grading three unique problems.

Since the official USAMO does not release standard solutions or grading schemes, we carefully developed a standardized grading scheme for each problem, drawing from reliable mathematical community resources, particularly the Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) forums.
Following USAMO conventions, each solution was graded out of a maximum of seven points with partial credit given for significant and meaningful progress.
The finalized grading schemes are available in our GitHub repository and displayed on our website.
We evaluate eight state-of-the-art reasoning models on the 2025 USAMO problems.
Each USAMO problem is scored out of 7 points, with a total maximum score of 42 points per run.
This model's performance is particularly noteworthy, as it can solve a problem correctly (scoring 6/7 or above) in six of its 24 attempts.

While current state-of-the-art LLMs achieve performance comparable to top human competitors on numerical-answer-focused competitions such as AIME and HMMT, our evaluation uncovers a significant gap in their ability to generate rigorous proofs.
In contrast, all evaluated LLMs consistently claimed to have solved the problems.
As detailed in Table 2, neither model accurately graded the solutions, consistently overestimating their quality.
Specifically, the models frequently awarded points for incorrect or unjustified reasoning, inflating the scores by a factor of up to 20.

we develop a grading pipeline based on LLM juries that aims to be as accurate and unbiased as possible. For the USAMO 2026, we still manually verified and adjusted the resulting grades

MathArena evaluates LLMs on recent math competitions, olympiads, and research problems. We use new problems to measure reasoning on questions that models have not seen during training. Each model runs four times on each problem.
The leaderboards show average scores and the average cost of a single run on one problem, in USD.
